topic: A tour guide in an old city
title: A Walking Tour of the Old Town

script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our walking tour of the old town. My name's Nadia and I'll be your guide for the next two hours.

We're standing in Market Square, which has been the centre of the town for over six hundred years. Farmers used to sell their animals here every Thursday, and there's still a food market here on Saturdays.
The tall building on your left is the old town hall. It was built in 1520, but most of it burned down in a fire in 1780 and had to be rebuilt.
If you look up at the clock tower, you'll notice that the clock has only one hand. That's because, at the time it was made, people didn't need to know the exact minutes!
In a moment we'll walk down that narrow street towards the river. Please be careful — the stones are uneven and can be slippery after rain.
We'll stop for twenty minutes at a traditional bakery, where you can try the local honey cake. Then we'll finish at the castle at around twelve. Any questions before we start?

script: Host: Welcome back to 'Better Habits'. My guest today is Dr Laura Kim, a sleep researcher. Laura, many people are proud of sleeping only five hours a night. Is that a problem?

Dr Kim: It's one of the most common myths I come across. A tiny percentage of people genuinely function well on very little sleep, but for the vast majority, regularly sleeping less than seven hours affects memory, mood and even the immune system.
Host: But surely you can catch up at the weekend?

Dr Kim: Partly, but not completely. Lie-ins can reduce tiredness, yet research shows that reaction times and concentration don't fully recover. It's a bit like trying to eat a week's worth of food on Sunday.
Host: What's the single biggest thing people can do to sleep better?

Dr Kim: Keep the same wake-up time every day, including weekends. Your body clock loves routine. The second thing would be to stop looking at screens for at least half an hour before bed — not just because of the light, but because scrolling keeps your brain alert.
Host: And what about naps?
Dr Kim: Short naps of around twenty minutes can be great, especially in the early afternoon. Longer than that, and you risk waking up groggy and finding it harder to sleep at night.
Host: Fascinating. Thanks, Laura.

script: Mark: I'm seriously thinking about getting an electric car, but I keep changing my mind.
Selin: What's putting you off?
Mark: Mainly the price. They're still quite a bit more expensive than petrol cars.
Selin: Up front, yes. But you have to look at the total cost. Charging at home costs a fraction of what you'd spend on petrol, and there's far less maintenance — no oil changes, fewer parts to break.
Mark: Fair point. But what about long journeys? I visit my parents twice a month and it's four hundred kilometres away.
Selin: Most newer models can do that on a single charge, or close to it. And if not, a fast charger gets you to eighty per cent in about half an hour — just enough time for a coffee.
Mark: I've also read that making the batteries is terrible for the environment.

Selin: It's true that battery production has a big carbon footprint, and mining the materials raises real concerns. But studies suggest that, over its lifetime, an electric car usually ends up cleaner — especially if the electricity comes from renewable sources.
Mark: So you'd go for it?
Selin: If you mostly drive in the city and can charge at home, I think it's a no-brainer. If not, maybe wait a couple of years until there are more chargers.

script: Thanks for coming. Every year, thousands of young people pay to volunteer abroad — building schools, teaching English or working in orphanages. The intention is almost always good. But tonight I'd like to encourage you to ask some difficult questions before you sign up.

First: who actually benefits? Some programmes charge volunteers several thousand dollars, yet only a small part of that money reaches the local community. Before you book, ask the organisation for a clear breakdown of costs.

Second: do you have the right skills? If you wouldn't be allowed to teach or build a wall in your own country without training, why should it be acceptable somewhere else? In some cases, unskilled volunteers take work away from local people who need the income.

Third, and perhaps most importantly, think about children. Short-term volunteers in orphanages can do real harm. Children become attached to adults who disappear after two weeks, again and again. Many child-protection experts now advise against this kind of volunteering altogether.

I'm not saying don't go. Volunteering can be life-changing for everyone involved — if it's done responsibly. Choose longer placements, use the skills you really have, and support projects that are run by local people. Thank you.

script: Today I want to look at one of the most puzzling phenomena in medicine: the placebo effect. A placebo, as you know, is a treatment with no active ingredient — a sugar pill, say, or a saline injection. And yet, in clinical trials, a substantial proportion of patients given placebos report genuine improvement.

Now, it would be easy to dismiss this as patients simply imagining they feel better. But brain-imaging studies have shown that placebos can trigger the release of the body's own painkillers — endorphins. In other words, the effect isn't merely 'all in the mind' in the dismissive sense; it has a measurable physiological basis.

What's particularly intriguing is how context shapes the response. Expensive placebos tend to work better than cheap ones. Injections outperform pills. Even the colour matters: in several studies, blue pills were perceived as more calming, red ones as more stimulating.

Perhaps most surprising of all are so-called 'open-label' placebos. Here, patients are told explicitly that the pill contains nothing — and yet, in trials for conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, many still improved. This suggests that the ritual of treatment itself, and the relationship with a caring practitioner, may be doing a good deal of the work.

Of course, we should be cautious. Placebos rarely shrink tumours or cure infections. Their effects are strongest for subjective symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue. But the implications for how doctors communicate with patients are, I'd argue, profound.

script: Interviewer: Five years ago, you sold most of your possessions and moved into a flat with just a hundred items. What prompted that?
Jonas: Burnout, essentially. I had a well-paid job, a big house, two cars — and I was miserable. I realised I was working longer hours to pay for things I barely had time to use.
Interviewer: Critics say minimalism is a luxury for people who can afford to throw things away and buy them back later.

Jonas: That's a fair criticism, and I don't dismiss it. It's much easier to own very little when you know you could replace something if you needed to. For people on low incomes, keeping things 'just in case' is often a perfectly rational strategy.
Interviewer: So what would you say to them?
Jonas: Honestly, I'd say the message isn't really for them. Minimalism, as I see it, is a response to over-consumption, and that's mainly a problem of the comfortably off.
Interviewer: Has it made you happier?

Jonas: Calmer, certainly. Happier... it's complicated. The first year was exhilarating. Then I found I'd simply replaced one obsession — buying things — with another — getting rid of them. These days I'm less strict. The question I ask isn't 'How few things can I own?' but 'Does this thing earn its place in my life?'
